lines.text: Wednesday, the fourth of October, nineteen sixty-seven. Shortly after eleven at night, a row of lights falls out of a clear, moonless sky toward a fishing harbour in Nova Scotia, and goes into the sea.
One light stays behind, floating on the water. Police watch it. Then it sinks. The navy sends divers. They search for three days, and they find nothing at all.
Canada's military then files the sighting as an unidentified flying object. That one word is why this is called Canada's Roswell.
But here is the problem with every famous mystery. Stories travel. Tonight we follow this one link by link, from a payphone to a government file, and check what each hand added.
Facts first, theories labelled. Message received. Link one.
Chapter one. The call. Shag Harbour is a village of a few hundred people at the southern tip of Nova Scotia, on a coast built for fishing and fog.
That night, five young people are driving home from a dance along Highway Three. At the wheel is Laurie Wickens, seventeen years old.
They see lights ahead, low over the water. Accounts differ on the number. Three, or four. Yellow, or white. All agree: a row, tilted, sinking toward the bay.
Then a small hill blocks their view for about ten seconds. When they can see the water again, the row of lights is gone. In its place, one white light, sitting on the surface.
Wickens stops at a phone booth and calls the police. By his own later account, the first question is whether he has been drinking.
Then the payphone rings. The police are calling him back. Other people have called too. Something, they now realise, really did come down.
Note what the first link actually carries. Not a spaceship. Not a crash. Just lights, a descent, and a light on the water. Everyone assumed the same thing: an aeroplane had gone down.
Wickens died only this year, aged seventy-six, still the face of the story. Link one is solid. Pass it on.
Chapter two. The shore. A corporal and two constables from the Mounties reach the water within fifteen or twenty minutes. They expect survivors.
They are in time to see it. A light on the water, about half a mile out, drifting with the ebbing tide. It stays for roughly five minutes. Then it goes out.
Constable Ron O'Brien told reporters it was being carried out to sea by the tide, and was gone before a boat could reach it. Trained observers. Same story as the teenagers.
Within minutes, a Coast Guard lifeboat from Clark's Harbour and six or more local fishing boats are on the water, hunting for a downed aeroplane.
They find no wreckage and no survivors. They find a patch of foam, thirty to forty yards wide by one account, at least eighty feet by another. Fishermen thought it was not ordinary tide foam.
Later retellings say the foam was yellow, bubbling, and smelled of sulphur, stretching half a mile. The reports from that week do not say that. It grows with each telling.
Now the first crack. The Colorado university investigators, who telephoned the police weeks later, wrote a line the legend leaves out: apparently no one actually saw anything enter the water.
One witness two miles away did see the descent. Three red-orange lights, moving at aircraft speed, with a whistling sound like a falling bomb. Then they dropped behind the houses.
By three in the morning, the boats come home. Link two is strong on the lights and on the light that floated. It is weaker on the object itself.
Chapter three. Halifax. At the Rescue Co-ordination Centre, the first job is simple: is any aircraft missing? By morning, the answer is no.
At ten twenty that morning, a priority telex goes to Ottawa. It carries the police account: a dark object, over sixty feet long, with four white lights, whistling as it came down.
It adds two things the teenagers never said. A bright flash when it hit the water. And a single light floating on the surface. Already, the story is bigger than the people who saw it.
It also contains the phrase that makes history. All conventional explanations, aircraft, flares and the like, are dismissed. The message is therefore headed: UFO report.
The telex gives a position: forty-three degrees thirty and a half minutes north, sixty-five forty-five west. Just outside Lower Woods Harbour, about two hundred and seventy metres offshore.
Here is what the Coast Guard cutter actually reported: many small boats, nil results. And, quote, all other possible leads, aircraft, flares, et cetera, checked, nil results.
Remember that line. Nil results means they found nothing. It does not mean they proved it was not a flare. That difference will matter in two links.
Chapter four. Ottawa and the Navy. The telex lands at the Air Force's air desk, the office that handles every UFO report in Canada.
Squadron Leader Bain tells the press the Air Force gets hundreds of reports every week, but this is one of the few where it might get something concrete.
He recommends an underwater search. The Navy tasks Fleet Diving Unit Atlantic. Two days after the sighting, divers reach Clark's Harbour.
Seven divers eventually search an area about half a mile by a mile and a half, in water nine to twenty metres deep. Flat sand. Good visibility.
They work through the weekend. If a sixty-foot machine, or even a large piece of one, had landed there, this is exactly the search that finds it.
At six thirty on Sunday, the eighth of October, the search ends. A handwritten note in the file says it in four words: terminated, nil results.
The Chronicle Herald reports it: not a trace, not a clue, not a bit of anything. In December, headquarters writes to two universities that the investigation ended without conclusive findings.
One more detail: in nineteen sixty-seven, about one hundred and ninety UFO reports reached Ottawa. Only nine were judged worth investigating. Shag Harbour was one. So officials did take it seriously.
Chapter five. The same night. Believers say that on the fourth of October, the whole region lit up. Other lights were seen. Here is the second place a message gets crowded.
At seven fifteen, an Air Canada crew over Quebec reported a bright, rectangular object with trailing lights, and two silent explosions. That is hundreds of kilometres from Nova Scotia.
Far out at sea, Captain Leo Mersey of the fishing boat Nickerson watched red flashing lights and four radar blips. Colorado's own notes put him about a hundred and seventy-five nautical miles away.
In Halifax, around ten, someone phoned a newsroom about a glowing object. Fine. Different place, different hour, different light.
Over the years, these reports were stitched into one night of UFOs. That makes the story feel stronger. It actually makes it weaker, because it hides which claim belongs to which witness.

But there is a fair question about the explosions. A bright meteor, a bolide, often breaks into a row of lights as it falls, at a shallow angle, looking slow. That fits the first part of the Shag Harbour lights.
It does not explain a light that floated on the water for minutes. A meteor is a good match for the fall. It is a poor match for the landing.
Chapter six. The lost link. Years later, the University of Colorado's UFO project, the Condon Committee, makes telephone calls about Shag Harbour. These notes survive.
The watch officer reads them a report in which the object, sixty feet long, exploded on hitting the water. The police corporal says no one actually saw anything go in.
Two accounts from the same chain of command. One says a flash on impact. One says the light went out, and ten minutes later officers were rowing to the site.
The Colorado notes add another line. The nearby Air Force radar station reported no unusual radar object, and no Canadian or American air operations in the area.
Which brings us to the sceptics' favourite: marine flares. Boats fire them as standard distress signals. They ignite late, fall in a row, and float on the water as they burn out.
Skeptoid's Brian Dunning argues a few flares, perhaps fired by a prankster, fit the descent and the floating light. He cannot prove it, and the file contains no matching boat.
Honest problem: the light reportedly lasted about five minutes on the water. Whether a single flare could burn that long, and then be carried by the tide, no one has settled.

And now the famous memo. Colonel Turner writes that the search centre had, quote, discounted the possibility of aircraft, flares, floats, or any other known objects. That became: the government ruled out flares.
Read it against the cutter's telex. The chain went from we checked and found nothing, to the government discounted every known object. A shrug became a verdict. That is the relay at work.
Chapter seven. The added link. In nineteen ninety-three, a quarter of a century later, the story takes a turn. A book is published: Dark Object.
Its authors, UFO researchers Chris Styles and Don Ledger, interview old witnesses and promise the world's only government-documented UFO crash.
Their new claim: the craft did not sink. It moved underwater, seventy kilometres up the coast to the naval base near Shelburne, where it was joined by a second craft before both flew away.
Shelburne was a real US-linked sonar station, and that sounds convincing. But nothing in the 1967 files, no ship's log, no radar record, mentions any of it.
The new material comes from witnesses recalled decades later. Memory does what the telex did: it smooths, adds and fills the gaps. Without a record from the time, that is a story, not evidence.

What about a secret military test? It is a popular fallback. But secret aircraft are tested in remote ranges, not low over a village with a dozen witnesses watching. Skeptoid calls it logically excluded.
Today the village keeps the memory. A lookout over the bay and a small UFO centre. For Shag Harbour, the mystery became a part of its identity.
Debrief. Time to score Shag Harbour.

Several independent witnesses saw lights descend toward the water: evidence. Police officers saw a light floating, then vanish: evidence. The foam as a physical trace: partial, since it was never tested. A craft or wreckage found by the navy: none.

The claim that the government ruled out flares: debunked, it came from a loose summary of a nil-results telex. A craft travelling underwater to Shelburne: unsupported. An extraterrestrial craft: no evidence.

The verdict. Real event, unidentified, not alien. Honest people saw lights come down, police saw one float, and Canada's military took it seriously enough to search. A fireball or flares remain the likeliest answers.
And the lesson is the relay. The core of the story survived four links intact. What did not survive was the memo's meaning, the foam's size, and the second craft.
Next case: December nineteen sixty-five, Kecksburg, Pennsylvania. Witnesses saw a fireball fall into the woods, and reports spoke of something shaped like an acorn. Was anything recovered?
What do you think came down at Shag Harbour? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for the next ancient mystery put to the test.
